decisions.location: Section 4 (Hofstede's Cultural Dimensions), pp. 74-75, lines 222-237; References, pp. 78-79, lines 500-531
decisions.quote:
Hofstede has collected data from a comprehensive study of how values in work place are influenced by culture. A 116000 questionnaires were distributed in 72 countries in twenty languages between 1967 and 1973. The survey started strictly using the employees of a large comparison; IBM. Later it has been enlarged using other foundations as well.
After analyzing this extensive work, Hofstede created an exemplary standard in culture classification. He developed four cultural dimensions that can be relied on to determine a country’s predominant disposition which could reflect its cultural tendencies. These cultural dimensions are: Power Distance (PDI), Individualism versus Collectivism (IDV), Masculinity versus Femininity (MAS), and Uncertainty Avoidance (UAI). Hofstede (1980, 1997) developed the subsequent description of Arab countries
decisions.reason: The primary text retests Hofstede's IBM Arab-country cultural-dimension scores (PDI = 80, UAI = 68, IDV = 91/38, MAS = 53; 116,000 questionnaires across 72 countries between 1967 and 1973) generalized to Jordan, attributing those scores in-text to Hofstede (1980, 1997) and Hofstede's (1980, 1991, 2005). However, the reference list omits Hofstede (1980) and contains no 1999 Hofstede entry (listing only 1991 and 1997 editions of Cultures and organizations: Software of the mind, while Culture's Consequences appears only inside Kirkman et al., 2006's review title). Although the blind coding of Hofstede, G. (1980) with an unfilled title is defensible under the printed-only extraction rule, that rule does not establish that the shipped row (Hofstede, 1999, Culture's consequences: International differences in work-related values) denotes a different empirical original, nor does the primary text establish whether 1999 reflects an equivalent printing/edition citation or a bibliographic error (and prior Luna's claimed 1999 reference quote is absent from the source text). Because neither bibliographic equivalence nor distinctness can be certified from the primary text alone, the original citation metadata is undeterminable and this edition/year ambiguity is retained for the parent.

decisions.location: Section 8 (Conclusion), p. 77, lines 479-488; Abstract, p. 71, lines 22-34
decisions.quote: The study has a rich insights into Jordanian national culture through questioning the generalization made by Hofstede (1980) that classify Jordan within the bundle of other Arab countries. Our findings support the opposite of Hofstede’s classifications. Jordanians were found to be slightly low on power distance, low on uncertainty avoidance, collectivist and feminine. Hofstede’s (1980, 1991, 2005) assumption that the passing of time does not change culture because changes are minor enough that do not influence country’s position relative to others, does not apply to his findings about Arab cultures and thus his generalization made to Jordanian culture is not validated.
decisions.reason: Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1 (author overall conclusion first), the authors state an explicit overall verdict in both the Abstract ('scores (findings) obtained by Hofstede in his previous studies conducted in Arab countries and then generalized to Jordanian culture are not scientifically valid') and the Conclusion ('Our findings support the opposite of Hofstede’s classifications... his generalization made to Jordanian culture is not validated'), as Jordanians scored low on PDI, UAI, and MAS rather than matching Hofstede's Arab-country profile. Because the paper explicitly attributes the same IBM Arab-country benchmark across Hofstede's 1980, 1991, 1997, and 2005 works, 'failed' is unambiguously supported for that single IBM Arab-country target (and must not be transferred to any different empirical original).

The replication text (Han et al., 2022) exclusively cites and re-tests the Molecular Psychiatry journal article Han et al. (2021a) ('Brain aging in major depressive disorder: results from the ENIGMA major depressive disorder working group', 10.1038/s41380-020-0754-0), applying its 19-cohort ridge regression model trained on 952 male and 1236 female healthy controls and comparing against its test sample of 2126 controls and 2675 MDD patients (+1.08 years higher brain-PAD, Cohen's d = 0.14, with no clinical moderators). Inspection of the newly supplied full primary texts for both the shipped 2018 Biological Psychiatry conference abstract (Schmaal et al., 2018, 10.1016/j.biopsych.2018.02.061) and Han et al. (2020/2021) shows that both come from the ENIGMA-MDD consortium with overlapping investigators, but the 2018 abstract used Gaussian Process Regression with 10-fold CV in 4708 controls and 2924 MDD patients, reported an internally contradictory result (0.75/0.64 years 'significantly lower than brain age gap estimates in healthy controls' in Results vs. 'brains of patients were estimated to be only <1 years older than healthy controls' in Conclusions) and preliminary clinical associations, and neither primary text provides a cohort crosswalk or explicit preliminary-publication link. Thus, equivalence versus distinctness between the shipped 2018 conference report and the cited 2021 journal article remains unresolved from primary evidence.

decisions.quote:
Conclusions
This study further validates our previously developed ENIGMA brain age algorithm. Importantly, we replicated the brain age gap in depression with a comparable effect size. Thus, two large-scale independent mega-analyses across in total 32 cohorts and >3400 patients and >2800 controls worldwide show reliable but subtle effects of brain aging in adult depression. Future studies are needed to identify factors that may further explain the brain age gap variance between cohorts.
decisions.reason: For the primary-selected journal article Han et al. (2021a; 10.1038/s41380-020-0754-0), the replication outcome in Han et al. (2022) is unambiguously 'successful' (+0.99 years higher brain-PAD in 766 MDD patients vs. 751 controls across 13 new cohorts, Cohen's d = 0.15, p = 0.005, with no clinical subgroup moderators, matching the journal article's +1.08 years, d = 0.14). However, under the scope rule that dependent outcomes must not be transferred to a different or unverified original, this journal outcome cannot be transferred to the shipped 2018 conference abstract (Schmaal et al., 2018; 10.1016/j.biopsych.2018.02.061), whose full primary text uses a different model and sample counts (Gaussian Process Regression on 4708 controls and 2924 MDD patients vs. ridge regression on 4314 total controls [2188 training/2126 test] and 2675 MDD patients), contains an internal direction contradiction between Results ('significantly lower' gap of 0.75/0.64 years) and Conclusions ('<1 years older'), reports preliminary clinical associations, and lacks a verified cohort crosswalk to the 2021 journal article. Because row 799's target identity equivalence is unresolved, the dependent row outcome is undeterminable pending parent identity resolution.

decisions.location: Discussion, paragraphs 1-2 and final summary paragraph, lines 90-91 and 97; Abstract, line 41
decisions.quote:
The general pattern of developmental changes in verbalization behaviors that Flavell et al. (1966) observed was upheld. However, it was clear from this much larger sample of children that even the youngest children exhibited more speech behavior than would have been expected based on the original work. According to the values in Table 2, 76% of our 5-year-old group vocalized at least sometimes, compared with 10% of Flavell et al.’s equivalent group.
Overall, the findings in this registered replication report tend to confirm the notion that children under 7 spontaneously apply speech to remembering. When examining the characterizations of observed verbalizations in Table 2, 167 out of 220 5-year-old children verbalized either “sometimes” or “usually”; however, our findings supported the original finding that the youngest children, the 5-year-olds, did verbalize significantly less than the 7- and 10-year-old children. While the youngest children verbalized less than the older children in the original Flavell et al.(1966) and in the current meta-analysis, we did not confirm that speech continues increasing from 7- to 10-year-olds in lab-level analyses.
decisions.reason: Evaluating the whole Abstract and Discussion/Summary under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1 shows that the authors' own overall synthesis is an explicit partial/mixed verdict rather than an unqualified whole-study success. In both the Abstract ('determined that the original pattern of findings was largely upheld: older children were more likely to verbalize, and their memory spans improved... However, unlike Flavell et al., substantial proportions of our 5- and 6-year-old samples overtly verbalized... Also, continuous increase in overt verbalization from 7- to 10-years-old was not consistently evident') and the Discussion/Summary ('replicated the spirit of Flavell, et al.’s (1966) original findings: the number of children spontaneously verbalizing increased from our youngest to our older age groups... However... First, very young children were found to verbalize in greater numbers than originally reported... Second, if there is an inflection point in the rate of verbalization development, it appears to occur prior to 7 years of age'), the colon explicitly defines what was upheld (the broad directional increase from age 5 to older children and the recall benefit of speech) while pairing it with explicit failures to confirm central tested components of Flavell et al.'s (1966) developmental trajectory (76% vs. 10% spontaneous verbalization in 5-year-olds—refuting the absence of speech before age 7—and no confirmed continuous increase between ages 7 and 10). Under Step 3 Rule 1, this explicit partial support ('largely upheld' / 'replicated the spirit' paired with central disconfirmed components) governs as 'mixed'.

decisions.location: Discussion, final conclusion paragraph (p. 1895, line 1, chars 31322-31630) and paragraphs 2-3 (pp. 1894-1895)
decisions.quote: To conclude, the current research has largely replicated the freezing-to-social-threat effect initially demonstrated by Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ). We hope our work strengthens the confidence in the effect and paves the way for further research and applications in the context of (social) threat and physiology.
decisions.reason: Reading the whole Discussion and final Conclusion under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1 (author overall conclusion first: 'If the authors state an explicit overall verdict for the original study, code that verdict directly and do not override it with individual sub-results') establishes 'successful'. The study's primary aim was to test whether Roelofs et al.'s (2010) heart-rate freezing response to angry faces is robust (noting that in Roelofs et al., 2010, the main effect of emotional expression on heart rate was marginal and only reached significance after adding STAI state anxiety as a covariate). Noordewier et al. (2019/2020) found a significant heart-rate deceleration to angry faces vs. happy and neutral faces even without STAI as a covariate (and relative to baseline), as well as significant STAI modulation when excluding one outlier, while not replicating the bivariate correlation between heart rate and STAI within the angry block. Across every synthesis passage—the Abstract conclusion ('In general, we thus find evidence for physiological signs of freezing in response to social threat'), Discussion paragraph 2 ('While our findings are not completely in line with Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ), they support the notion that people show physiological signs of freezing in response to social threat'), Discussion paragraph 3 ('These findings add critically to the robustness of the finding that social threat adds to parasympathetically driven heart rate deceleration—relevant for freezing (and without having to add STAI as covariate to the statistical model)'), and the Final Conclusion ('To conclude, the current research has largely replicated the freezing-to-social-threat effect initially demonstrated by Roelofs et al. ( 2010 ). We hope our work strengthens the confidence in the effect')—the authors treat the target finding of Roelofs et al. (2010) as replicated overall. Under Step 3 Rule 1, this explicit whole-study replication verdict governs over the secondary covariate-correlation contrast.
